newsitem.title: USA: U.S. dollar been strong "for some time" - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: U.S. dollar been strong "for some time" - Rubin.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Friday reiterated his support for a strong dollar but added that the U.S. currency has been strong "for some time now.
"A strong dollar is in the U.S. interest," Rubin told a news conference ahead of Saturday's meeting of the Group of Seven nations in Berlin, adding: "We've had a strong dollar for some time."
His remarks seemed to signal a subtle shift in the Clinton administration's perceived public policy toward the dollar.
Every time that Rubin spoke out in favor of a strong dollar, currency dealers read that as U.S. backing for an ever-stronger currency and acted accordingly in the market.

But Rubin himself has been consistently careful to steer clear of saying he wanted a stronger dollar -- as opposed to a strong one -- and his remarks on Friday seemed designed to draw that to the market's attention.

Rubin said that he expects foreign exchange issues to be a "principal topic" of discussion at Saturday's meeting of economic policymakers from the G7--Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
"Some G7 countries have expressed concern about the recent declines in their currencies," Rubin said. "We look forward to discussing these issues in Germany."
Rubin declined to say, in response to a question, whether the orderly reversal of the dollar that the G7 first sought in April 1995 is now over. Since then, the U.S. currency has risen sharply.

As he has done before, Rubin said that ultimately, currencies and other markets reflect fundamentals. "It is crucial to concentrate on the objectives of balanced growth and low inflation in all countries of the G7," he said.
Rubin said that the U.S. economy was "performing well." But the prospects in Japan and Europe are "somewhat less clear," he said.

"In Japan, the main challenge is to maintain a supportive macro-economic environment to meet Japan's commitment to a strong domestic demand-led recovery and to consolidate the gains made in reducing external imbalances," he said.

Rubin refused to prescribe a specific policy mix for Tokyo. Some analysts have voiced concern about Japan's plans to sharply tighten its budget policy, including raising its consumption tax, at a time when its economy is weak.
Rubin said that Japan needed to continue to open its markets to foreign goods. At a minimum, though, "you don't want them to backtrack," the U.S. Treasury chief said.

Rubin said the United States also has a "critical interest" in a strong and dynamic Europe. He said he looked forward to discussing with his European counterparts the implications for the world economy of the upcoming monetary union there.

Other issues that will be discussed in Berlin, according to Rubin, include Russia's economy, ongoing reform of the international financial institutions and measures to improve safeguards against systemic risk in the world financial system.
